items.title: Exact symmetry and an observed object
items.student: Use ideal figures with these complete descriptions: a6cmby4cmrectangle,a4cmsquare,an equilateral triangle,a scalene triangle with vertices(0,0),(4,0),(1,2),and a circle. Draw or sketch each and identify every line of symmetry,stating a count and reason. For a centred square include diagonal as well as horizontal/vertical lines. If a safe teacher-selected desk object is available,observe it and distinguish an ideal model from manufacturing/shape deviations;otherwise mark object observation NOT OBSERVED. Do not collect glass,sharp litter or objects outside the approved area. For an ideal2cmby3cmby4cmcuboid,describe one plane of symmetry halfway between opposite faces and distinguish this3Dplane from a line on a2Dfigure.
items.teacher: Counts:rectangle2,square4,equilateraltriangle3,scalenetriangle0,circleinfinitely many diameter lines. The scalene triangle has unequal side lengths4,√5,√13,so no reflection symmetry. A real object may only approximately match an ideal figure. Every line must map the whole shape onto itself;an arbitrary line through the centre is not automatically a symmetry line except for the circle. The unequal-edge cuboid has three central symmetry planes,each halfway between a pair of opposite faces and parallel to them. A plane is a flat two-dimensional surface in the solid;it is not merely a line on a drawing.

items.title: An actual plane mirror and a mathematical prediction
items.student: Teacher supplies an approved plane mirror,preferably acrylic,and a small labelled object on a paper surface. Mark the mirror line and place the object3cm in front along a perpendicular. Individually predict the image location,then actually view and sketch the apparent image when equipment is provided. Describe whether it is in front or behind the mirror,and distinguish the virtual image from a physical object that could be touched behind it. Use the plane-reflection model to label equal perpendicular distances;do not claim a direct ruler measurement of an inaccessible virtual point. Teacher records observed/not observed action. If no mirror is provided,complete only the paper prediction and mark actual observation NOT OBSERVED.
items.teacher: For an ideal plane mirror,the image appears3cm behind the mirror at equal perpendicular distance,is upright and the same size;it is virtual,not a physical object behind the surface. This is a plane-mirror model,not a rule for every curved driving mirror. Actual observations are learner/teacher records,not invented results. Keep mirrors stable,avoid broken glass and do not direct bright sunlight into eyes.

items.title: Fold a line into a perpendicular bisector
items.student: Draw equal-unit axes and triangleA(1,1),B(4,1),C(2,3). The mirror line isx=0. On thin paper,fold along the line and trace corresponding vertices when teacher-provided materials permit;otherwise draw the coordinate construction and mark tracing NOT OBSERVED. Join each object vertex to its image and locate the midpoint. State what happens to distances,angles,points on the mirror and clockwise/counterclockwise order of the labelled triangle. No cutting is required.
items.teacher: A′(−1,1),B′(−4,1),C′(−2,3). Each joining segment is perpendicular to the mirror and bisected by it;points on the line remain fixed. Corresponding lengths and angles are preserved,so the figures are congruent. Reflection reverses the orientation of the ordered vertex correspondence;it is not a translation or a180°rotation. Actual folding/tracing must be observed separately from coordinate correctness.

items.title: Horizontal and vertical mirror lines
items.student: Use equal-unit axes. ReflectP(0,1)andQ(3,−1)inx=2;reflectR(2,3)andS(−1,−1)iny=−1. Separately reflect triangleT(0,0),U(2,0),V(1,2)iny=1. Draw the mirror lines and join corresponding vertices. Explain the fixed point and the formulas x′=2a−x,y′=y forx=a,andx′=x,y′=2b−y fory=b.
items.teacher: P′(4,1),Q′(1,−1),R′(2,−5),S′(−1,−1);S lies on its mirror. Triangle imagesT′(0,2),U′(2,2),V′(1,0). Equal perpendicular distances justify each formula. The unchanged coordinate is parallel to the mirror;do not reverse both coordinates for every reflection.

items.title: Diagonal reflections are not negative enlargements
items.student: Reflect triangleA(2,−1),B(3,1),C(1,4)firstiny=xandseparatelyiny=−x. Plot and label both images on equal-unit axes. State the coordinate rules,verifyP(2,2)isfixediny=xandQ(2,−2)isfixediny=−x. Compare the reflection of(3,1)iny=−xwith its signed-factor−1enlargement about the origin.
items.teacher: Iny=x,the rule(x,y)→(y,x) gives(−1,2),(1,3),(4,1). Iny=−x,the rule(x,y)→(−y,−x) gives(1,−2),(−1,−3),(−4,−1). P andQ are fixed on their stated lines. The point(3,1)reflects to(−1,−3),but a factor−1enlargement sends it to(−3,−1). Swapping-and-negating is different from negating both coordinates.

items.title: Find a mirror line from two point pairs
items.student: TriangleA(0,0),B(2,0),C(0,1) maps by one reflection toA′(−1,1),B′(−1,3),C′(0,1). Plot all points. Find midpoints ofAA′andBB′,construct their perpendicular bisectors with ruler/set square,and check they give one mirror line. Determine its equation using the midpoint coordinates,rise/run and intercept. Check every pair and explain why the fixed pointC alone would not determine the line.
items.teacher: Midpoints(−0.5,0.5)and(0.5,1.5)lie on y=x+1. Each joining segment has slope−1,and the line through its midpoint with slope1 is perpendicular. The rule(x,y)→(y−1,x+1)checks all three pairs,including fixedC(0,1). A single fixed point lies on many possible lines,so it cannot uniquely identify the mirror. The construction,not a memorised origin-only rule,determines this shifted line.

items.title: A mirror line with a different slope
items.student: One reflection mapsP(1,1)toP′(5,3)andQ(0,3)toQ′(4,5). On equal-unit axes,find both midpoints and construct perpendicular bisectors using a ruler/set square. Identify the common line. Use the two midpoint coordinates to find rise/run and the equation y=mx+c. Verify it bisects both segments at right angles. Linear-line scaffolding:between two different x values,m=change iny/change inx;then substitute one point to findc.
items.teacher: MidpointsM(3,2),N(2,4);m=(4−2)/(2−3)=−2,c=8,so y=−2x+8 or2x+y=8. PP′andQQ′both have changes(4,2),slope1/2,perpendicular to slope−2;midpoints lie on the derived line. This is the same perpendicular-bisector condition as axis/diagonal mirrors,with a different slope. All coordinates and correspondence are supplied;no general reflection-formula lookup is required.

items.title: Congruence and labelled orientation
items.student: Use triangleA(0,0),B(3,0),C(1,2). Copy/plot its direct imageA′(2,1),B′(5,1),C′(3,3)and opposite imageA″(0,0),B″(−3,0),C″(−1,2),using the stated correspondenceA→A′orA″,etc. Compare corresponding lengths,angles and clockwise/counterclockwise order. With teacher-provided paper shapes or safely precut labelled copies,check superposition with and without turning over;record actual cutout use separately. Explain why identical area alone cannot prove congruence.
items.teacher: The first image is a translation by(2,1),so direct congruence preserves labelled orientation. The second is reflection inx=0,so opposite congruence reverses it. Both preserve corresponding lengths/angles. Do not change the correspondence by relabelling to hide the orientation distinction. For example a2by6rectangle and3by4rectangle both have area12but are not congruent. Paper coordinate work does not certify unobserved cutout handling.

items.title: Establish SSS and SAS with complete data
items.student: Pair1:trianglesABCandDEF haveAB=DE=3cm,BC=EF=4cm,CA=FD=5cm. Pair2:AB=DE=4cm,AC=DF=6cm,and the included anglesAandD are50°. Draw or construct the two cases with ruler/protractor as supplied,compare correspondence,and name/justify a sufficient congruence test for each. Explain why SAS requires the angle between the two given sides. Merely saying two sides and any angle is not the same criterion.
items.teacher: Pair1 SSS;all three corresponding side lengths match. Pair2 SAS;the given50°angle is betweenAB/ACandDE/DF. Each case fixes a triangle up to direct/opposite placement. General SSA is not a sufficient congruence criterion;some particular SSA data may determine a triangle,but that is not a universal test. Do not infer congruence from a sketch’s appearance rather than the supplied measurements.

items.title: Two angles and the corresponding side
items.student: CaseA:angleA=angleD=40°,angleB=angleE=65°,andAB=DE=5cm. CaseB:angleA=angleD=40°,angleC=angleF=75°,andAB=DE=5cm. For each,find the third angle and state whether the side is included between the two originally given angles. Explain why both supply sufficient congruence information when correspondence is kept. Compare two triangles with the same40°,65°,75°angles but correspondingABlengths5cmand10cm.
items.teacher: CaseA:thirdangle75°,included sideAB/DE,ASA. CaseB:remainingB/E65°,AB/DE is not between the originally givenA/CandD/Fangles,AAS/SAA;after finding the third angle it can also be justified through ASA. The same-angle triangles with corresponding lengths5and10are similar but not congruent. AAA fixes shape but not size. Every side statement must refer to corresponding vertices.

items.title: Why RHS is a right-triangle criterion
items.student: TrianglesABCandDEF are right-angled atCandF,with hypotenusesAB=DE=5cm and corresponding legsAC=DF=3cm. Identify the right angles,hypotenuses and given matching legs;find the remaining legs and justify congruence. Would a right angle and one leg alone suffice? Compare right triangles with legs3and4versus3and5. Then make a four-test checklist for SSS,SAS,ASA/AAS andRHS,including the essential condition for each.
items.teacher: RemainingBC=EF=4cm byPythagoras;RHS gives congruence. The special right-angle/hypotenuse/side information is sufficient even though it is not the general SAS arrangement. A right angle plus one leg is insufficient:the3by4and3by5leg triangles have unequal other legs and are not congruent. Checklist:three corresponding sides;two sides and included angle;two angles and a corresponding side;or right angle,equal hypotenuse and corresponding leg.

items.title: Use reflection and congruence responsibly
items.student: Write a short advice card for a classmate with two specific checked uses:one ideal plane-mirror/reflection example andone congruent-copy/stencil example justified by a valid triangle test. Include the limit that many driving mirrors are curved,so the plane-mirror equal-size coordinate model does not apply automatically. Discuss road-safety uses only as a classroom example;no road visit or driving instruction. If approved digital plotting is supplied,enter triangle(1,1),(3,1),(2,3),reflect iny=0,record the real tool/inputs/output and check on paper. If no device is supplied,mark digital reflection NOT OBSERVED. Share the advice only when directed,andrecordactualsharing separately.
items.teacher: Example:the ideal plane mirror predicts an image at equal perpendicular distance;congruent3–4–5triangle stencil copies can be checked bySSS. Digital expected image(1,−1),(3,−1),(2,−3);a written coordinate answer alone does not prove tool use. A convex driving mirror often changes image size/field of view and must not be presented as a plane congruence model. Accept varied specific correct advice with evidence and limits;do not invent digital actions,external safety results or an actual presentation.

items.title: Independent final reflection and congruence data
items.student: Use only this final card and separate prompts. Ideal figures:a6by4rectangle and a square. Plane-mirror pointP(3,1),mirrorx=0. Reflect triangleA(1,1),B(3,1),C(2,3)iny=−x. Separate unknown-mirror pairs:U(0,0)→U′(−2,2),V(2,0)→V′(−2,4). Congruence cases with correspondenceABC↔DEF: S:AB=DE=4,BC=EF=5,CA=FD=6; T:AB=DE=4,AC=DF=6,angleA=angleD=50°; W:angleA=angleD=40°,angleB=angleE=70°,AC=DF=5; H:rightanglesCandF,hypotenuseAB=DE=5,legAC=DF=3; N:bothtriangles haveangles40°,60°,80°but no side data. Units for sides arecm. Use ruler,set square/protractor and equal-unit axes as supplied. No teaching cards,peers or worked keys.
